questions.q: A model's error is very high, but the derivative of the error at the current weight is almost 0. What does that tell you?
options: The error curve is nearly flat here, for example a plateau, so the slope gives little guidance even though the error is high
The model has reached its best possible weight
The error must be about to fall to zero
The derivative has been computed incorrectly, because high error always means a steep slope
questions.why: A derivative measures slope, not height. A flat stretch can sit at a high error. Treating "slope near 0" as "we are at the minimum" is the classic confusion between a function's value and its slope.

questions.q: Using the power rule, what is the derivative of f(x) = x³ at x = 2?
questions.why: Bring the power down and reduce it by one: f′(x) = 3x², so f′(2) = 3 × 4 = **12**. 8 is the value f(2), not the slope; 6 forgets to square x; 4 uses the x² rule (2x) by mistake.

questions.q: A chai stall sells 1,200 − 20p cups a day at price ₹p, and each cup costs ₹10. Profit is π(p) = (p − 10)(1,200 − 20p). At what price is the derivative zero?
questions.why: Expand: π(p) = −20p² + 1,400p − 12,000, so π′(p) = −40p + 1,400. Setting it to zero gives p = **₹35** (daily profit 25 × 500 = ₹12,500). ₹30 is the answer for the chapter's original demand of 1,000 − 20p; ₹60 is where demand hits zero, which earns nothing.

questions.q: For f(x) = x² at x = 5, the chord slopes with nudges h = 1, 0.1 and 0.01 come out as 11, 10.1 and 10.01. What is f′(5)?
options: 11, the first chord slope
10.01, because the smallest nudge is exact
10, the value the chord slopes are heading towards
25, the value of the function
questions.why: The pattern is 10 + h, so as h shrinks the chord slope approaches **10** (and the power rule confirms 2 × 5 = 10). Any fixed h, however small, still measures an average over a short stretch, which is why 10.01 is close but not the derivative.

questions.q: You find a point where the derivative of the loss is exactly 0. What can you conclude?
options: It is definitely the minimum
The curve is flat there; it could be a minimum, a maximum or a saddle
It is definitely the maximum
The loss is zero at that point
questions.why: A zero derivative only says "flat here". For a bowl such as (w − 3)² the flat point is the minimum, but on other curves it can be a hilltop or a flat ledge. Assuming zero slope means minimum is the common slip, and zero slope says nothing about the loss being zero.

questions.q: For one positive example, log-loss is L(p) = −ln p, where p is the predicted probability. What is dL/dp at p = 0.5?
questions.why: The derivative of ln p is 1/p, so dL/dp = −1/p = −1/0.5 = **−2**. The negative sign says raising p lowers the loss. +2 drops the minus sign; −0.693 is ln 0.5, the value of the log rather than its slope.

questions.q: The tangent to f(x) = x² at x = 3 is y = 6x − 9. Using the tangent, what is the best estimate of f(3.2), and how close is it?
options: 10.2, just below the true value 10.24
9, because the tangent touches the curve at (3, 9)
19.2, by multiplying the slope by 3.2
10.24 exactly, because the tangent equals the curve
questions.why: 6 × 3.2 − 9 = **10.2**, very close to the true 3.2² = 10.24. The tangent is the best straight-line approximation near the point, not an exact copy of the curve, so the small gap grows as you move further away. 19.2 forgets the −9 intercept.

questions.q: Interview: "Why do derivatives matter for training a machine learning model?" Which answer is best?
options: They compute the model's accuracy on the test set
They are only needed for neural networks, not for linear models
They guarantee the model finds the global minimum
The derivative of the loss with respect to a weight tells you which way to nudge that weight, and roughly how much the loss will change, so you can improve it step by step
questions.why: The sign gives the direction (positive slope: decrease the weight) and the size gives the strength of the effect, which is exactly what gradient descent uses. Derivatives give no guarantee of a global minimum on non-bowl-shaped losses, and linear and logistic regression use them too.
